tip: Italian builds should from the conditional of dovere (must): dovrei studiare = I should study.
Avere bisogno takes di, so the relative pronoun carries that di with it: ciò di cui ho bisogno = the thing I need.
Reflexive verbs take essere, so the past-perfect is mi ero svegliato with ero, and svegliato agrees with the speaker.
Con i quali is a formal stand-in for con cui, and quali agrees with what it refers to: plural masculine colleghi gives i quali.
After quando for a finished future action, Italian uses the future perfect avrò finito, while the main clause ti chiamo stays present.
Va fatto is literally goes done, and andare plus a past participle means must be done: questo lavoro va fatto subito.
Italian stacks negatives: non ... mai is literally not ... never, yet non avevano mai assaggiato just means had never tasted.
A past main verb like volevo pulls the following subjunctive into the past, so it is venissi, not venga: volevo che tu venissi.
Arrivare forms its past with essere, so ero appena arrivato is literally I was just arrived where English says I had just arrived.
You can mix time frames: se avessi studiato is a past condition, but ora sarei preparato gives a present result.
Bisogna never takes a subject; the one must sense is built into the verb: bisogna fare attenzione = one must pay attention.
Use bisogna che plus the subjunctive when the need targets a specific person: bisogna che tu parta subito.
English says I want you to come, but Italian cannot use an infinitive across two subjects: it needs voglio che tu venga.
Venire a sapere is literally to come to know, and it means to find out: venne a sapere la verità = he found out the truth.
Viene chiusa is a passive with venire that stresses the event happening; essere, la porta è chiusa, would describe a state instead.
The se-clause takes the subjunctive fossi, never the conditional: it is se fossi te, and se sarei is the classic mistake.
Italian frames cannot as not managing to: non riesco a dormire is literally I do not succeed in sleeping, using riuscire, not potere.
Essere da plus an infinitive means still to be done: il progetto è da rifare says the project is to be redone, it still needs it.
Avere da plus an infinitive lists what you must do; ho da fare on its own also just means I am busy.
Andare plus a past participle carries obligation: questa storia va raccontata means the story must be told.
That non after a meno che is a filler, not a real negative: a meno che non cambi idea just means unless I change my mind.
When the hotel is only hoped for, not a specific one, the relative verb goes subjunctive: cerco un hotel che abbia, not che ha.
A command reported with dire turns into di plus an infinitive: ho detto di non preoccuparsi = I told him not to worry.
Continua a piovere da tre giorni uses the present with da where English switches to has been raining for three days.
The future can express a guess about the present, not future time: saranno le tre means it must be about three now.
Each verb fixes its own preposition before an infinitive, and continuare locks in a: continuare a discutere = to keep arguing.
Farsi plus an infinitive means getting something done for you: mi sono fatto aiutare da un esperto = I got an expert to help me.
Mettersi a is literally to put yourself to something, marking a sudden start: si è messo a ridere = he burst out laughing.
Cercare alone means to look for, but cercare di plus an infinitive means to try to: cerco di capire = I am trying to understand.
Sebbene always takes the subjunctive, even about real facts: sebbene il viaggio sia stato lungo reports a trip that truly was long.
Where English says reproached me for not having done, Italian uses di plus a past infinitive: di non averla avvisata.
In reported speech, here-words shift to there-words: qui becomes lì, so qui si mangia bene turns into lì si mangiava bene.
Andare plus a past participle expresses obligation: queste regole vanno rispettate means the rules must be respected by all.
Stare per plus an infinitive means to be on the verge of doing something: sto per partire = I am about to leave.
Lasciarsi plus an active infinitive means letting it happen to you: si è lasciato convincere = he let himself be convinced.
Andare a trovare someone means to go visit them, not to go find: sono andato a trovare i miei genitori = I went to visit my parents.
Italian can front the pronoun and tag the noun on as an afterthought: L'ho già letto, questo libro, where l' points ahead to libro.
Andare plus an -ndo verb means to go around doing it, ongoing and repeated: andavano dicendo = they kept saying.
Avere da fare means to be busy with things to do, not the English have to do of obligation: hanno da fare tutto il giorno.
Avere plus a noun plus da plus an infinitive can mean opportunity, not duty: abbiamo molto da imparare = we have much to learn.
Use chiedere che plus the subjunctive when you name who must act: ha chiesto che tutti fossero presenti, versus chiedere di plus infinitive.
Mettersi a plus an infinitive marks buckling down to something: mi sono messo a studiare seriamente = I got down to studying seriously.
Può darsi is literally it can give itself and means maybe; può darsi che then takes the subjunctive: può darsi che il museo sia chiuso.
An impersonal è plus an adjective plus che forces the subjunctive: è necessario che tutti partecipino, not partecipano.
The subjunctive fosse signals the speaker is not vouching for the claim: sosteneva che fosse impossibile leaves the truth open.
In reported speech a present statement backshifts to the imperfect: direct sono stanco becomes ha detto che era stanco.
